title: How to Review AI Theme Suggestions and Decide Which to Accept
summary: AI suggests new themes, merges and structural fixes for your feedback taxonomy. How to check the evidence, read the impact score, and decide what to accept.
body_markdown:
Your feedback taxonomy was right when you built it. Then customers started describing a new problem, a product shipped, and a chunk of your feedback stopped landing anywhere useful. AI can find those gaps and propose fixes: a new theme for comments nobody is capturing, a merge for two themes that say the same thing, a move for a sub-theme under the wrong parent.


Thematic surfaces these as a prioritized list of[suggestions inside the Themes Editor](https://help.getthematic.com/article/214-themes-editor-ai-suggestions) , each with an Apply and a Dismiss button and an estimate of how many comments it would affect. Deciding which to accept is your job, and it decides whether your taxonomy gets better or just gets bigger. The short version: check the evidence behind a suggestion before you read its impact score, treat the impact percentage as volume rather than importance, and remember you have four possible responses, not two.


Whether that upkeep amounts to[manual theme tuning](https://getthematic.com/insights/does-thematic-require-manual-theme-tuning) is a separate question, answered elsewhere. This piece is about what to do with the suggestions you get.


Below is the five-step process, the judgement call behind each of the six suggestion types, and the mistakes that turn a review into a rubber stamp.


## The five-step review process


1. Read what the suggestion is actually proposing, by category.
2. Check the evidence before you look at the estimate.
3. Read the impact percentage as volume, not importance.
4. Choose one of four actions, not two.
5. Batch the changes, apply once, and keep the rollback open.


## Step 1: Read what the suggestion is proposing


Thematic's Themes Editor runs 18 evaluation checks across your theme hierarchy and your untagged comments, split into 12 structural checks and 6 discovery checks at three context levels. The output lands in two tabs. Discover holds suggestions that increase coverage. Improve fixes the structure you already have.


Six categories come out of that, and each needs a different question from you:


- **New Phrases.** Untagged comments that match an existing sub-theme but aren't being captured, such as 50 comments mentioning "bill pay" that aren't tagged under your "Bill Payment" theme. Ask: is this genuinely the same topic, or a near neighbor that deserves its own theme?
- **New Themes.** A cluster of untagged comments on a topic you have no theme for, such as 30 comments about "two-factor authentication." Ask: is this durable, or a one-week spike from a single incident?
- **Organization.** A sub-theme filed under the wrong base theme, such as "Mobile App Crashes" under "Billing" instead of "App Experience." Ask: is it misplaced, or deliberate because of how your teams report?
- **Merges.** Two semantically similar sub-themes that could be combined, such as "Bill Payments" and "Payment of Bills." Ask: do different teams act on these two separately?
- **Mappings.** A merged theme assigned to the wrong sub-theme, such as "App crash" merged into "App Features" instead of "App Bugs." Ask: does the mapping match how the phrase is actually used in your comments?
- **Generic themes.** Themes too vague to be useful, such as "General Issues" or "Other Feedback." Accepting removes them. Ask: is this vague, or a deliberate catch-all that measures what your taxonomy is missing?


The pattern across all six: the AI can see your data. It can't see your business. A suggestion that's technically correct about the text can still be wrong about your organization.


## Step 2: Check the evidence before you look at the estimate


The fastest way to turn review into[rubber-stamping](https://getthematic.com/insights/human-review-ai-insights-automation-bias) is to read the AI's description and nothing else. Open the mapped phrases behind the suggestion, then read a sample of the comments it would retag. Thematic shows you both, which is what makes this a real check rather than a guess.


This matters more than it sounds. In a[field experiment with 228 evaluators](https://www.hbs.edu/ris/Publication%20Files/25-001_75068eb2-d475-4889-b341-aeabab6ef6d1.pdf) , researchers at Harvard Business School found that evaluators given an AI's written rationale were 11.9 percentage points less likely to correct the AI when it was wrong. When the AI recommended rejection, they were 14.7 points less likely. The researchers concluded that narratives "suppress productive overrides by substituting persuasive text for independent verification." A well-written suggestion is more persuasive, not more correct.


So read the comments, not the summary. If the sample doesn't look like one topic to you, the suggestion is wrong no matter how reasonable the description sounds.


## Step 3: Read the impact percentage as volume, not importance


Thematic estimates the percentage of comments each suggestion would affect. Sorting by that number finds what deserves your attention first. It isn't a ranking of what's safest to accept. High impact means high reward and a wide blast radius at once.


Two corrections to apply:


- **A low-impact suggestion can matter more than a high-impact one.** A change affecting 0.3% of comments on a theme that appears in your board deck outranks a 12% change on a theme nobody reads. Thematic's own guidance is to set[minimum coverage thresholds of 3% to 5%](https://getthematic.com/insights/ai-powered-customer-feedback-theme-discovery) to avoid chasing statistical noise. A suggestion that pushes a theme across that line changes what you can report, not just what you can see.
- **More themes isn't automatically better coverage.**[Research on taxonomy evaluation](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2502.11890) makes the trade-off explicit. Increasing granularity raises coverage by broadening definitions, but worsens balance by splitting volume across more categories. As that research puts it, "a greater number of categories does not guarantee comprehensive coverage." Accepting every New Theme suggestion raises your tagged percentage and can still leave you with a taxonomy nobody can report from.


The number that anchors the session is your overall coverage. Thematic's guidance on[building a taxonomy](https://getthematic.com/insights/how-to-build-a-customer-feedback-taxonomy) is that at least 80% of feedback usually falls into repeating themes, and Discover suggestions are what move that figure.


## Step 4: Choose one of four actions, not two


The two buttons suggest a binary. Thematic supports more than that, and most good decisions live in the middle:


- **Apply as proposed** , when the evidence matches and the naming fits how your teams talk.
- **Apply the substance, change the label.** Take the coverage gain, then[rename the theme](https://getthematic.com/insights/customize-ai-themes-customer-feedback) to your business language before committing the draft.
- **Restructure instead.** A misplaced sub-theme can move to the right base, start a new base, or be deleted. A mismerged theme can move, be deleted, or split into a new sub-theme. The AI's proposed destination is a starting point.
- **Dismiss** , when the suggestion is wrong for reasons the model can't see.


Dismiss a suggestion when it would do any of these:


- Merge two themes that different teams act on separately.
- Create a theme below your reporting threshold.
- Collapse a distinction your taxonomy encodes deliberately.
- Rename a theme a live dashboard depends on.


Thematic remembers dismissals and avoids resurfacing the same recommendation, so a dismissal is a durable instruction rather than a one-time skip.


## Step 5: Batch, apply once, keep the rollback open


Applying a suggestion stages it into your themes draft. It doesn't retag anything yet. The data changes only when you run the standard Apply flow. That's what makes batching the right default: work through a set of suggestions, commit them together, then review the result as a whole. Batching also keeps your[trend lines comparable](https://getthematic.com/insights/keep-feedback-trend-lines-comparable) across the change.


Three things to hold on to:


- Discard the draft to undo anything you haven't committed. After committing, Revert Draft restores any of the last three applied versions, showing who applied each and when.
- Thematic saves edits to a draft automatically and takes up to five minutes to apply a committed set. You get an email when the new themes are live.
- Sampling is deliberately randomized, so a second run surfaces different patterns rather than the same list. Regenerate clears your dismissals and starts fresh, which is rarely what you want mid-session.


Then measure yourself. NIST's[AI Risk Management Framework](https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/ai/NIST.AI.100-1.pdf) recommends collecting "data about the frequency and rationale with which humans overrule AI system output in deployed systems." If you accepted everything last quarter, your review isn't working as a control. NIST is blunt[elsewhere](https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/SpecialPublications/NIST.SP.1270.pdf) that human-in-the-loop practices "are not intended to serve as a form of oversight" on their own, and that without procedural support, expectations of human governance "are not borne out in practice."


## A worked example


A New Zealand retail and trade co-operative runs a three-person insights team against roughly 20,000 verbatim comments a month from 84 stores. A team that size can't read a month of feedback, let alone audit a taxonomy by hand. After setup, the team took basic training on the theme editor and took over the final customizations themselves.


That's the shape this review process is built for. The suggestion list does the scanning three people can't do across 20,000 comments. The three people do the part the model can't. They decide that "delivery delay" and "delivery damage" stay separate because different teams own them. They decide a new theme about a one-off outage isn't durable enough to keep. They catch the merge that would break a store-level report somebody relies on every Monday.


## Common mistakes to avoid


- **Accepting in list order.** The list is prioritized by estimated impact, not by confidence. Work Discover first for coverage, then Improve for structure.
- **Reading the description instead of the comments.** The description is the AI's case for itself. The comments are the evidence.
- **Treating one-click Apply as permission to skip the check.** One-click accept exists to make review fast, not optional.
- **Accepting a rename without checking downstream.** A theme name can be live in a dashboard, a BI model, or a quarterly commitment.
- **Running a review once and never again.** After applying a batch and retagging, open the panel again. The hierarchy has changed, so the checks find different things. New suggestions also keep appearing because[customer language keeps shifting](https://getthematic.com/insights/keep-ai-themes-accurate-language-changes) .


## The short answer


AI can propose improvements to your feedback themes across six categories, covering gaps in coverage and faults in structure, and estimate how much of your data each change would touch. Deciding which to accept is a verification job, not a sorting job. Open the evidence, read the impact number as volume rather than importance, use all four responses, and batch your changes so a wrong call is cheap to undo. The taxonomy stays yours. The AI just tells you where to look.
